new_entities.name: Low vitamin B12
new_entities.description: Subnormal vitamin B12 status measured by serum B12 or related functional biomarkers.

edges.effect_quant: Prospective cohort evidence is inconsistent for serum B12 alone, but low to low-normal B12 status in Framingham predicted faster MMSE decline and low B12 with high folate in pooled cohorts was linked to worse cognition (AOR 3.45, 95% CI 1.60 to 7.43).
edges.mechanism: Vitamin B12 is needed for myelin maintenance and one-carbon metabolism, so prolonged deficiency can plausibly affect cognition through methylation stress, homocysteine elevation, and neuronal dysfunction. The challenge is that serum B12 is an imperfect biomarker, which weakens the apparent signal in some cohort studies.
edges.summary: Low B12 status is a plausible cognitive risk factor, but the direct epidemiology is more mixed than many simple health claims suggest. The best summary is that conventional serum B12 alone has not shown a uniformly strong prospective association, yet lower or low-normal B12 repeatedly travels with worse cognitive trajectories in some older cohorts, especially when folate status is high or metabolic markers suggest functional deficiency.
edges.caveats: This edge is intentionally conservative because biomarker choice matters a great deal: methylmalonic acid and holotranscobalamin often perform differently from serum B12 alone. It should be read as a potentially meaningful but measurement-sensitive cognitive risk signal rather than a settled population-wide causal claim.

evidence.citation: OLeary F et al 2012 Br J Nutr
evidence.notes: Vitamin B12 status, cognitive decline and dementia: a systematic review of prospective cohort studies.

evidence.notes: Vitamin B-12 and folate status in relation to decline in scores on the mini-mental state examination in the framingham heart study.
